your plot of predictions, your data frame should vary your meanNDVI
numeric vector with both Archery == 1 and Archery == 0. In other words,
create a data frame with expand.grid( ):

newDats <- expand.grid(MeanNDVI = MeanNDVI.std,
Archery = factor(c("0", "1"),levels = c(0,1)))

And then add the other variables at their mean
newDats$Slope <- 0
newDats$FireDist <- 0
newDats$HorseDistCenter <- 0
newDats$AveRdDist <- 0
newDats$Date <- 0

Then make your predictions:
NDVI.predict <-modavgPred(cand.set = List, newdata = newData2,

parm.type = 'lambda',
level = 0.85, type = "response")

Best,

Ryan,

Your original plot looks correct to me based on your model results.

Ignoring covariates unrelated to your question, your equation for abundance will look like this (where x is your data):

y = exp(Intercept + Archery*x_archery + meanNDVI*x_ndvi + Archery:MeanNDVI*x_archery*x_meanNDVI)

Your equation at an Archery site  (x_archery = 1) will be

y = exp(-0.62 + 0.84 * (1) + 0.94 * x_ndvi + -0.83 * (1) * x_ndvi)

or

y = exp(0.22 + 0.11 * x_ndvi)

So there is still a positive relationship (0.11) with NDVI, it's just not as strong as sites that where preArchery, which again matches your figure.

Ken

messages.subject: AHM2's CAR models in NIMBLE (and in parallel)
messages.subject_clean: AHM2's CAR models in NIMBLE (and in parallel)
messages.body_plain:
Kéry & Royle (2021) Applied Hierarchical Modeling Vol.2 (AHM2) includes 5 spatial auto-regressive CAR models, 2 in chapter 3 and 3 in chapter 9. The code is available at the AHM_code GitHub repository <https://github.com/mikemeredith/AHM_code>.

Since JAGS will not do spatial auto-correlation models, these were coded in good ol' WinBUGS 1.4. WinBUGS is specific to the Windows OS. It is no longer maintained, and is not guaranteed to work on future Windows upgrades. The relatively new NIMBLE package will do spatial models, and I have 'translated' the WinBUGS code to run with nimble::nimbleMCMC. See the files tagged "..._nimble.R" here and here.

These models mix poorly and long runs are required, taking up to 5 days. It makes sense to run chains in parallel and to use as many cores as possible. Unlike jagsUI::jags, neither R2WinBUGS::bugs nor nimble::nimbleMCMC has built-in capability for parallel processing. Multiple instances can, however, be run in parallel using the CRAN package foreach. I've added code to implement this to the scripts in the AHM_code repository. See more information on using foreach here <https://mmeredith.net/blog/2021/parallel_chains_foreach.htm>.

The model in section 9.5 caused problems. In WinBUGS, it often throws an error, "Undefined real result". Kéry & Royle advise retrying multiple times. With foreach, with the argument .errorhandling='remove', it's easy to discard chains that throw errors and recover the results of those that run properly.

With this model, NIMBLE does not throw an error but prints a warning, "logProb is -Inf". It runs, but some of the random walk samplers are stuck at their starting values (with acceptance rate 0). The problem occurs when several of the starting values generated automatically by NIMBLE are far out in the tails of the posterior distribution, so that the probability of the model is effectively zero.

I identified and discarded the "stuck" chains and looked at the posterior distributions of the top-level stochastic nodes from those that worked. Based on that information, I added values to the inits function, with random draws from uniform distributions somewhat wider than the CrIs of the posteriors. The model than ran properly. Hi Simone,

My understanding is that mclapply() starts by assigning NULL to all elements of the output list. As it is running the job, if any of the parallel worker processes fail for some reason, nothing will be returned and the corresponding list element will remain NULL (apparently with no warning). Parallel workers could fail for a variety of reasons that depend on your exact hardware setup. Probably the most likely is that they run out of memory. The fact that you are seeing this happen randomly is good evidence to me that it is a memory issue. I'd consider trying fewer cores so that each core has more memory available.

Ken

Simone,

Is there a particular reason why you are using mclapply()? Forking is known to have mysterious problems that are hard to troubleshoot. See e.g. the Warning on the ?mclapply home page:

"It is strongly discouraged to use these functions in GUI or embedded environments, because it leads to several processes sharing the same GUI which will likely cause chaos (and possibly crashes). Child processes should never use on-screen graphics devices."

You can use socket clusters and parLapply instead. Your code also does not seem to set random numbers for the parallel processes, which can be potentially dangerous (i.e. identical samples). Neither mclapply nor parLapply takes care of the parallel numbers for JAGS, and JAGS's initialization is independent of how seed is set in the R process. It is a pet peeve of mine, I know, and others don't seem to care that much, but a great deal of thought was put into this by Martyn Plummer, and it is good practice to follow defaults put in place by a software's creator.

Some refactoring was done in rjags to expose the initialization part, which is used in dclone::parallel.inits that is used in a couple of downstream functions for convenience. So it is safe to do something like this:
library(dclone)
ncl <- 3
cl <- makePSOCKcluster(ncl)
clusterEvalQ(cl, library(dclone))
parLoadModule(cl, "glm")
pm <- jags.parfit(cl, data, "beta", model, n.chains=ncl)
stopCluster(cl)

Alternatively, if you want to monitor and possibly sample further:
cl <- makePSOCKcluster(ncl)
parJagsModel(cl, name="res", file=model, data=data,
    n.chains = ncl, n.adapt=1000)
parUpdate(cl, "res", n.iter=1000) # burnin
m <- parCodaSamples(cl, "res", jpara, n.iter=2000)
# you can keep sampling here until you shut down the cluster
stopCluster(cl)

Cheers,

Peter

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
Peter Solymos kindly suggested a way to tackle the problem I had of independent parallel jobs (thanks Peter!). I paste here below his reply.
Regards,
Simone

----
If the parallel jobs are independent you should be able to specify the data as a list, and then passing the list elements as data to the parLapply function, RNG should be fine because you can initiate the chains from the same call. If the data sets are really different in sample size the DAG graph size will be different and computing time will vary so you can use parLapplyLB which uses load balancing and fills in idle nodes.

library(dclone)

## your models
mod_fun <- function() {
    for (i in 1:N) {
        Y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], tau)
        mu[i] <- alpha + beta * (x[i] - x.bar)
    }
    x.bar <- mean(x[])
    alpha ~ dnorm(0.0, 1.0E-4)
    beta ~ dnorm(0.0, 1.0E-4)
    sigma <- 1.0/sqrt(tau)
    tau ~ dgamma(1.0E-3, 1.0E-3)
}

## data generation
set.seed(1234)
N <- 100
alpha <- 1
beta <- -1
sigma <- 0.5
x <- runif(N)
linpred <- crossprod(t(model.matrix(~x)), c(alpha, beta))

Y1 <- rnorm(N, mean = linpred, sd = sigma)
Y2 <- rnorm(N*2, mean = -linpred, sd = 2*sigma)
## list of data for the model
Data <- list(
  data1=list(N = N, Y = Y1, x = x),
  data2=list(N = N*2, Y = Y2, x = c(x, x))
)
## what to monitor
par <- c("alpha", "beta", "sigma")

test <- jags.fit(Data[[1]], par, mod_fun)
test <- jags.fit(Data[[2]], par, mod_fun)

## set up cluster
cl <- makeCluster(length(Data))

clusterEvalQ(cl, library(dclone))
clusterExport(cl, c("par", "mod_fun"))

Mods <- parLapply(cl, Data, function(d) {
  jags.fit(d, par, mod_fun, n.chains = 3, n.update=100, n.iter=100)
})

stopCluster(cl)

## you can also use a function if you'd like to save the output
## instead of passing it back to the main process:
## dname is the data set name from the list
## this is safer because you won't loose results that are already done

par_fun <- function(dname) {
  out <- try({
    m <- jags.fit(Data[[dname]], par, mod_fun,
                  n.chains = 3, n.update=100, n.iter=100)
    save(m, file=paste0(dname, ".RData"))
  })
  !inherits(out, "try-error")
}

cl <- makeCluster(length(Data))
clusterEvalQ(cl, library(dclone))
clusterExport(cl, c("par", "mod_fun", "Data"))
## this is where files will be saved
clusterEvalQ(cl, getwd())

OK <- parLapply(cl, names(Data), par_fun)

stopCluster(cl)

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Evan H. C. Grant (USGS) and I are looking for a postdoctoral researcher to work with us on a project related to disease and decision-making (details below). We would greatly appreciate it if you could circulate the ad below to anyone you think would be interested.

Thank you!

Grace

Postdoctoral researcher position: Improving disease management decisions

in the face of uncertainty

Massachusetts Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit (MA Coop Unit)

University of Massachusetts, Department of Environmental Conservation, Amherst, MA

Review of applications will begin 01 May 2021

Position start date Summer/Fall 2021

Position description The USGS Cooperative Ecosystems Studies Unit at the University of Massachusetts, in collaboration with the USGS Eastern Ecological Science Center are seeking to recruit a postdoctoral researcher that will develop quantitative tools to improve decision-making for the high-profile emerging pathogen of amphibians, Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans (Bsal). The challenge is identifying a mitigation strategy that accommodates tradeoffs in other components of the system and accounts for differences in risk. For example, when faced with the potential threat of disease emergence, resource managers must balance: (a) the risk of declines following a disease outbreak if management is delayed, and (b) the potential for harm to the system of implementing unnecessary management if no disease outbreak occurs. This work addresses a need to builds upon a previous effort that framed the decision related to a possible Bsal invasion with three National Wildlife Refuge managers in the northeastern United States (a hotspot for Bsal risk). This work is a collaboration between the USGS Amphibian Research Monitoring Initiative and the Massachusetts Cooperative Research Unit. The postdoctoral researcher will use simulations, modeling, and optimization to identify a suitable set of actions for wildlife disease decisions when there are multiple objectives and complex risk profiles. The postdoctoral researcher will generate user-friendly visualization tools intended to support management decisions. This project will help to understand, predict, and communicate the tradeoffs decision-makers are forced to make in the face of uncertainty for this and other emerging wildlife disease threats.

We highly encourage people from historically underrepresented groups to apply. The postdoc will work closely with collaborators from the USGS and Refuge managers. Please note that the successful candidate will likely work remotely until it is determined by USGS that offices are safe to be occupied.

The University of Massachusetts, Amherst (which ranks among the top public universities nationally) and the USGS Eastern Ecological Science Center at the SO Conte Anadromous Fish Research Lab are located in Western Massachusetts. The area offers a rich cultural environment in a rural setting close to major urban centers, with many great outdoor recreational opportunities.

Salary/Benefits The postdoctoral researcher will be provided:

1.     Annual salary of $55,000 plus benefits

2.     Travel funds to attend a national conference

3.     Working alongside professionals that encourage work-life balance, promote mental health well-being, and focus on helping you achieve your career goals

4.     Professional development relevant to a career with the USGS but transferable to other agencies

5.     Mentoring, encouragement, and autonomy to ensure that they see and understand how their perspectives are vital to achieving the mission of the USGS

Duties The postdoctoral research will be expected to

1.     Build a simulation model that includes ecological processes (e.g., survival, recruitment, etc.), downstream effects of Bsal on human society (e.g., park visitation rates, public engagement, etc.), and National Refuge Manager risk profiles,

2.     Conduct a sensitivity analysis to each of several pathogen invasion scenarios, and

3.     Build a user-friendly decision tool to aid managers in understanding how the potential management actions change as a function of elements of the decision and ecological system (i.e., using the results of the sensitivity analysis).

Eligibility

-   PhD in ecology, decision science, epidemiology, biology, math, statistics, wildlife, or other related field

Qualities of preferred applicants The following will be considered positive factors in choosing a successful candidate. We do not expect applicants to have all of these qualities and is not meant to discourage applicants.

-       Good writing and communication skills

-       Desire and ability to publish in peer-reviewed journals

-       Independent and motivated

-       Skills in simulation modeling, statistics, and/or optimization

Application To apply, please submit your application as a single PDF with the document name “YOUR LAST NAME-Bsal postdoc app- 2021.pdf” in an email with the subject “Bsal postdoc application” to Dr. Graziella DiRenzo at gdir...@umass.edu. Please include in your application the following materials:

(1) a 300–600 word cover letter describing your research interests and background, why you are interested in this position, and your career goals;

(2) a curriculum vitae or resume;

(3) the contact information (name, position, relationship to applicant, email, and phone number) for three references;

Please send questions to any of the project investigators listed below.

Project investigators

Dr. Graziella DiRenzo (gdir...@umass.edu), U.S. Geological Survey, MA Coop Unit

Dr. Evan H. C. Grant (ehg...@usgs.gov), U.S. Geological Survey, Eastern Ecological Science Center
